metadata.description: Comprehensive FODMAP food classification database for Crohn's disease management
primary_sources: Varney et al. (2017) - FODMAP content of commonly eaten foods
Tuck & Barrett (2017) - Fermentable short chain carbohydrate (FODMAP) content of common food
Cox et al. (2020) - FODMAP diet in IBD randomized trial (Gastroenterology)
Zhan et al. (2018) - Diet Advice for Crohn's Disease: FODMAP and Beyond (Nutrients)
metadata.notes: Serving sizes based on Monash University guidelines where available. FODMAP ratings use Monash traffic light system: LOW (green), MODERATE (amber), HIGH (red). Crohn's-specific notes added for post-resection and flare considerations.

fodmap_types_legend.fructose: Excess fructose (monosaccharide) - fructose in excess of glucose
fodmap_types_legend.fructans: Fructans (oligosaccharide) - chains of fructose molecules, includes inulin and FOS
fodmap_types_legend.GOS: Galacto-oligosaccharides - found in legumes and some nuts
fodmap_types_legend.sorbitol: Sugar alcohol polyol - found in stone fruits
fodmap_types_legend.mannitol: Sugar alcohol polyol - found in mushrooms, cauliflower, watermelon

fruits.name: Apple (all varieties)
fruits.crohns_notes: High in insoluble fiber (skin). If tolerated post-reintroduction, peel and cook to reduce fiber load.

fruits.name: Apricot
fruits.crohns_notes: Stone fruit; high sorbitol. Dried apricots are even higher FODMAP.

fruits.name: Avocado
fruits.crohns_notes: Excellent healthy fat source for Crohn's patients who often need calorie-dense foods. Very high in sorbitol at larger serves. Good post-resection if tolerated - soft, nutrient-dense.

fruits.name: Banana (unripe/firm)
fruits.crohns_notes: Excellent for Crohn's. Easy to digest, binding effect helps with diarrhea. Part of the BRAT diet. Ripe bananas become moderate-high FODMAP due to increased fructans.

fruits.name: Banana (ripe)
fruits.crohns_notes: As bananas ripen, starch converts to fructans. Stick to firm/slightly green bananas during elimination.

fruits.name: Blackberry
fruits.crohns_notes: Seeds may irritate inflamed bowel. Avoid during flares.

fruits.name: Blueberry
fruits.safe_serving: 1/4 cup (40g) conservative; up to 125g per Monash 2024 update
fruits.crohns_notes: Excellent choice - anti-inflammatory antioxidants. Low fiber per serving. Monash increased safe serving in recent update.

fruits.name: Cantaloupe / Rockmelon
fruits.crohns_notes: Good hydration source. Soft texture, easy to digest.

fruits.name: Cherry
fruits.crohns_notes: Very high in sorbitol. Even small amounts may trigger symptoms.

fruits.name: Clementine
fruits.crohns_notes: Good vitamin C source. Remove membrane/pith if bowel is sensitive.

fruits.name: Coconut (fresh flesh)
fruits.crohns_notes: Good fat source. Desiccated coconut also low FODMAP.

fruits.name: Cranberry (fresh/dried unsweetened)
fruits.crohns_notes: Watch for added sweeteners in dried versions (often contain apple juice or HFCS).

fruits.name: Date
fruits.crohns_notes: Calorie-dense, useful if underweight. High in natural sugars.

fruits.name: Dragon fruit / Pitaya
fruits.crohns_notes: Seeds are small but numerous; may irritate strictured bowel.

fruits.name: Fig (fresh)
fruits.crohns_notes: Very high fructose. Seeds may cause issues with strictures.

fruits.name: Grapefruit
fruits.crohns_notes: CAUTION: Interacts with many medications including immunosuppressants (azathioprine, cyclosporine). Check with pharmacist.

fruits.name: Grape (red and green)
fruits.crohns_notes: Skins may be harder to digest. Consider peeling if bowel is sensitive.

fruits.name: Guava (ripe)
fruits.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A (ripe). Unripe guava is HIGH FODMAP.
fruits.crohns_notes: Must be fully ripe. Rich in vitamin C.

fruits.name: Honeydew melon
fruits.crohns_notes: Good hydration. Keep to safe serving as fructose rises quickly.

fruits.name: Kiwi (green)
fruits.crohns_notes: Contains actinidin enzyme which aids protein digestion. Natural mild laxative effect - may help Crohn's patients with constipation-predominant symptoms.

fruits.name: Lemon / Lime
fruits.crohns_notes: Safe flavor enhancer. Can replace garlic/onion flavor in cooking.

fruits.name: Lychee
fruits.crohns_notes: Very high in polyols.

fruits.name: Mandarin / Tangerine
fruits.crohns_notes: Excellent choice. Easy to peel, low fiber.

fruits.name: Mango
fruits.crohns_notes: Can be included at very small serving. Rich in vitamin A.

fruits.name: Nectarine
fruits.crohns_notes: Stone fruit - high sorbitol.

fruits.name: Orange
fruits.crohns_notes: Good vitamin C source. Remove pith/membrane if inflamed bowel. Orange juice limited to 100ml.

fruits.name: Papaya / Paw paw
fruits.crohns_notes: Contains papain enzyme which aids digestion. Excellent choice for Crohn's patients - soft, easy to digest.

fruits.name: Passion fruit
fruits.crohns_notes: Seeds are hard; strain if strictures present.

fruits.name: Peach
fruits.crohns_notes: Stone fruit - high sorbitol.

fruits.name: Pear
fruits.crohns_notes: Among highest FODMAP fruits. Contains both excess fructose AND sorbitol.

fruits.name: Persimmon
fruits.crohns_notes: Can form bezoars (phytobezoars) in stomach; extra caution post-surgery.

fruits.name: Pineapple (fresh)
fruits.crohns_notes: Contains bromelain (anti-inflammatory enzyme). Good for Crohn's. Canned in juice also OK at 1/2 cup drained.

fruits.name: Plantain
fruits.crohns_notes: Excellent starchy carb for Crohn's. Cook well. Used in SCD and anti-inflammatory diets.

fruits.name: Plum
fruits.crohns_notes: High sorbitol. Prunes (dried plums) are even higher.

fruits.name: Pomegranate
fruits.crohns_notes: Seeds may cause mechanical obstruction with strictures.

fruits.name: Raspberry
fruits.crohns_notes: Seeds may irritate inflamed bowel. Strain for puree if needed.

fruits.name: Rhubarb
fruits.crohns_notes: Often requires added sugar to be palatable. Use safe sweeteners.

fruits.name: Strawberry
fruits.crohns_notes: Good choice. Seeds are tiny and generally well tolerated.

fruits.name: Tangelo
fruits.crohns_notes: Good citrus option.

fruits.name: Watermelon
fruits.crohns_notes: Contains both excess fructose and mannitol. One of the highest FODMAP fruits.

fruits.name: Dried fruit (general - raisins, sultanas, currants, dates, prunes)
fruits.safe_serving: Raisins: 1 tbsp (13g) is low. Most others avoid.
fruits.high_fodmap_threshold: >13g raisins; most dried fruits HIGH at any serve
fruits.crohns_notes: Concentrated sugars and fiber. Generally avoid during flares and post-resection.

vegetables.name: Artichoke (globe)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Very high fructans. Jerusalem artichoke is even higher.

vegetables.name: Asparagus
vegetables.crohns_notes: Tough, fibrous texture. Difficult to digest post-resection.

vegetables.name: Bean sprouts
vegetables.crohns_notes: Low fiber, easy to digest. Good choice.

vegetables.name: Beetroot (fresh/raw)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Canned/pickled beetroot is lower FODMAP than fresh. Cooking method matters.

vegetables.name: Beetroot (canned/pickled)
vegetables.crohns_notes: FODMAPs leach into canning liquid. Drain well.

vegetables.name: Bell pepper / Capsicum (green)
vegetables.crohns_notes: May cause gas for some. Roasting and peeling improves digestibility.

vegetables.name: Bell pepper / Capsicum (red)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Slightly higher FODMAP than green pepper. Roast and peel for best tolerance.

vegetables.name: Bok choy / Pak choi
vegetables.crohns_notes: Excellent choice. Good calcium source (important for Crohn's patients on corticosteroids).

vegetables.name: Broccoli (heads/florets)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Heads are lower FODMAP than stalks. Cook well to soften fiber. May cause gas even at safe serving.

vegetables.name: Broccoli (stalks)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Higher in fructans than the heads. Peel tough outer layer.

vegetables.name: Brussels sprouts
vegetables.crohns_notes: Gas-producing even at low FODMAP serves. May not be tolerated during flares.

vegetables.name: Butternut squash / Pumpkin
vegetables.crohns_notes: Cook until very soft. Purees well for easy digestion post-resection.

vegetables.name: Cabbage (common, red)
vegetables.crohns_notes: May cause gas. Cook well. Savoy cabbage is higher FODMAP - avoid.

vegetables.name: Carrot
vegetables.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - low FODMAP at all tested servings
vegetables.crohns_notes: Excellent staple. Cook well for easier digestion. Safe during flares when cooked soft.

vegetables.name: Cauliflower
vegetables.crohns_notes: High in mannitol. Gas-producing. Cauliflower rice may be tolerated at small serving due to smaller pieces cooking more thoroughly.

vegetables.name: Celeriac / Celery root
vegetables.crohns_notes: Good potato substitute when cooked into mash.

vegetables.name: Celery
vegetables.crohns_notes: Very stringy fiber. Avoid if strictures present. Cooking does not significantly reduce mannitol.

vegetables.name: Chives
vegetables.crohns_notes: Safe onion/garlic flavor substitute.

vegetables.name: Corn / Sweet corn
vegetables.high_fodmap_threshold: >1 cob; creamed corn is HIGH FODMAP
vegetables.crohns_notes: Indigestible cellulose hull. May appear undigested in stool - this is normal. Chew well. Avoid with strictures.

vegetables.name: Cucumber
vegetables.crohns_notes: Peel if skin causes issues. Good hydration source.

vegetables.name: Eggplant / Aubergine
vegetables.crohns_notes: Skin can be tough. Peel for better tolerance.

vegetables.name: Fennel bulb
vegetables.crohns_notes: Fennel tea (strong) is high FODMAP. Bulb is OK at safe serving.

vegetables.name: Garlic
vegetables.safe_serving: AVOID entirely during elimination. Use garlic-infused oil instead.
vegetables.crohns_notes: Fructans are water-soluble but NOT oil-soluble. Garlic-infused oil is safe because fructans don't transfer to oil. Critical to avoid garlic powder and garlic salt too.

vegetables.name: Ginger (fresh root)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Anti-nausea and anti-inflammatory properties. Excellent for Crohn's patients. Helps with medication-induced nausea.

vegetables.name: Green beans / String beans
vegetables.crohns_notes: Cook until very soft. Remove strings if present.

vegetables.name: Kale
vegetables.crohns_notes: Very high in insoluble fiber raw. MUST cook for Crohn's patients. Raw kale salads not recommended post-resection.

vegetables.name: Leek (green leaves only)
vegetables.safe_serving: Green part only, up to 1 cup
vegetables.crohns_notes: WHITE/BULB PART IS HIGH FODMAP (fructans). Only use the dark green leaves.

vegetables.name: Leek (white bulb)
vegetables.crohns_notes: High fructans like onion.

vegetables.name: Lettuce (all varieties - iceberg, butter, romaine, rocket/arugula)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Iceberg is easiest to digest. Raw salads may be difficult during flares - consider cooked/wilted.

vegetables.name: Mushroom (button, shiitake, portobello, enoki, etc.)
vegetables.safe_serving: Canned champignon: 1/2 cup (75g) is low FODMAP
vegetables.high_fodmap_threshold: Fresh mushrooms: any serving of most varieties
vegetables.crohns_notes: All fresh mushrooms high in mannitol. Canned/drained mushrooms are lower due to mannitol leaching into liquid. Oyster mushroom may be tolerated at small serve (1 cup).

vegetables.name: Okra
vegetables.crohns_notes: Mucilaginous texture may soothe gut. Cook well.

vegetables.name: Olive
vegetables.crohns_notes: Good healthy fat source. Easy to digest.

vegetables.name: Onion (brown, white, red, shallot)
vegetables.safe_serving: AVOID entirely during elimination. Use onion-infused oil.
vegetables.crohns_notes: One of the highest FODMAP foods. Fructans are water-soluble but NOT oil-soluble. Onion-infused oil provides flavor without FODMAPs. Check all processed foods for onion powder.

vegetables.name: Parsnip
vegetables.crohns_notes: High fiber when raw. Cook until very soft for best tolerance.

vegetables.name: Peas (green/garden)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Small serving OK. Skins may be hard to digest.

vegetables.name: Potato (white, all varieties)
vegetables.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - low FODMAP at all tested servings
vegetables.crohns_notes: Excellent safe staple for Crohn's. Easy to digest when peeled and cooked. Mashed potatoes are very well tolerated post-resection.

vegetables.name: Radish
vegetables.crohns_notes: Mild peppery flavor. Raw may be hard on inflamed bowel.

vegetables.name: Scallion / Spring onion (green part only)
vegetables.crohns_notes: WHITE/ROOT PART IS HIGH FODMAP (fructans like onion). Only use the green tops.

vegetables.name: Snow peas / Mange tout
vegetables.crohns_notes: Very small safe serving. Sugar snap peas are also high FODMAP.

vegetables.name: Spinach (baby)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Good iron source. Cook to reduce oxalates and improve iron absorption. Important for Crohn's patients who are often iron-deficient.

vegetables.name: Squash / Zucchini / Courgette
vegetables.crohns_notes: Peel for easier digestion. Makes good noodle substitute (zoodles).

vegetables.name: Sweet potato / Kumara
vegetables.crohns_notes: Becomes moderate FODMAP at 100g and high above that. Good nutritional density at safe serving. Mash for best tolerance.

vegetables.name: Tomato (common, fresh)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Acidic - may irritate if mouth ulcers or fistulas present. Cooking reduces acidity slightly. Remove seeds/skin if needed.

vegetables.name: Tomato (canned)
vegetables.crohns_notes: Base for many sauces. Check for added onion/garlic in canned varieties.

vegetables.name: Tomato paste / Concentrate
vegetables.crohns_notes: Concentrated - small amounts pack flavor. Check for garlic/onion in ingredients.

vegetables.name: Turnip / Swede
vegetables.crohns_notes: Cook until soft. Good mash ingredient.

vegetables.name: Water chestnut
vegetables.crohns_notes: Crunchy texture; chew well.

vegetables.name: Yam
vegetables.crohns_notes: Good starchy staple. Easy to digest when cooked.

grains_and_cereals.name: Amaranth flour
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Despite being gluten-free, still high FODMAP.

grains_and_cereals.name: Barley
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Contains gluten AND fructans. Avoid.

grains_and_cereals.name: Buckwheat (groats and flour)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Naturally gluten-free despite the name. Good nutrient profile.

grains_and_cereals.name: Bulgur wheat
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Small serve is OK. Still contains gluten.

grains_and_cereals.name: Corn / Maize (flour, starch, polenta)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Cornflour is a safe thickener. Polenta/grits are excellent soft-texture options.

grains_and_cereals.name: Cornflakes (plain, no HFCS or inulin)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Check ingredient list for chicory root / inulin / FOS which are high FODMAP additives.

grains_and_cereals.name: Couscous
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Made from wheat semolina. High fructan.

grains_and_cereals.name: Freekeh
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Wheat-based. High fructans.

grains_and_cereals.name: Millet
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Gluten-free. Easy to digest when cooked well.

grains_and_cereals.name: Oats (rolled/steel-cut)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Soluble fiber source - generally well tolerated. Oat porridge is soothing. Avoid flavored varieties with added HFCS or fruit.

grains_and_cereals.name: Pasta (wheat-based)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Small serving is OK during elimination. Cooking and cooling pasta increases resistant starch.

grains_and_cereals.name: Pasta (gluten-free, rice/corn-based)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Ensure no added legume flour (chickpea pasta is HIGH FODMAP). Rice and corn pasta are safe.

grains_and_cereals.name: Quinoa
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Complete protein (all essential amino acids). Excellent for Crohn's patients. Rinse before cooking to remove saponins.

grains_and_cereals.name: Rice (white, brown, basmati, jasmine, wild)
grains_and_cereals.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - low FODMAP at all tested servings
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Safest grain for Crohn's. White rice is easiest to digest. Brown rice has more fiber - use during remission. Part of BRAT diet.

grains_and_cereals.name: Rice noodles / Vermicelli
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Easy to digest. Good alternative to wheat noodles.

grains_and_cereals.name: Rice cakes / Rice crackers
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Check for added onion/garlic flavoring.

grains_and_cereals.name: Rye
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Very high fructan content. Rye bread and rye crispbread are high FODMAP.

grains_and_cereals.name: Sorghum
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Gluten-free ancient grain. Good alternative.

grains_and_cereals.name: Sourdough bread (spelt, traditional long-ferment)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: MUST be traditionally fermented (long, slow rise). The fermentation process breaks down fructans. Mass-produced 'sourdough' is NOT the same - check ingredients. True sourdough only has flour, water, salt, starter.

grains_and_cereals.name: Sourdough bread (wheat)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Wheat sourdough is lower FODMAP than regular wheat bread but higher than spelt sourdough.

grains_and_cereals.name: Spelt flour (non-sourdough)
grains_and_cereals.safe_serving: Not recommended unless in sourdough form
grains_and_cereals.high_fodmap_threshold: Any normal serving of non-fermented spelt
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Spelt is only low FODMAP when fermented as sourdough bread.

grains_and_cereals.name: Tapioca / Cassava flour / Starch
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Good thickener and baking ingredient. Easy to digest.

grains_and_cereals.name: Wheat bread (standard white/wholemeal)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: One slice is OK during elimination. Standard serving of 2+ slices is high FODMAP.

grains_and_cereals.name: Wheat flour (plain/all-purpose)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Small amounts in recipes (e.g., as thickener) may be tolerated.

grains_and_cereals.name: Popcorn (air-popped)
grains_and_cereals.crohns_notes: Hulls can irritate inflamed bowel. Avoid during flares and with strictures.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (cow, regular)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Many Crohn's patients are lactose intolerant. Lactase enzyme supplements can help.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (lactose-free cow)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Good calcium and protein source. Important for Crohn's patients on corticosteroids (bone density).

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (goat)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Still contains lactose despite common misconception.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (almond, unsweetened)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Usually fortified with calcium and vitamin D. Good choice.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (coconut, canned)
dairy_and_alternatives.safe_serving: 1/2 cup (120ml); light version OK at 3/4 cup
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Good for cooking. Calorie-dense (helpful if underweight).

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (coconut, carton/beverage)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Much more dilute than canned. Check for inulin/chicory additives.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (oat)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Very small safe serving. Not suitable as a glass of milk substitute.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (rice)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Low protein and nutrient content. Consider calcium-fortified versions.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (soy, made from soy PROTEIN/isolate)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: CRITICAL: Must be made from soy PROTEIN ISOLATE, not whole soybeans. Check label. US brands commonly use whole soybeans (HIGH FODMAP).

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (soy, made from whole soybeans)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Most US brands are made from whole soybeans. Must check ingredient list for 'soy protein isolate' vs 'whole soybeans' or 'soybeans'.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (macadamia)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Good alternative. Check for inulin additives.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Milk (hemp)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Good omega-3 source.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Yogurt (regular cow)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Contains live cultures which may benefit gut microbiome, but lactose is problematic.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Yogurt (Greek, plain)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Straining removes some lactose. Very small safe serving. Lactose-free Greek yogurt is preferred.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Yogurt (lactose-free)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Excellent choice. Probiotics benefit gut microbiome. Important for Crohn's patients.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Yogurt (coconut, plain)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Check ingredients carefully. Many brands add inulin/chicory fiber for texture which is high FODMAP.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (hard/aged: Cheddar, Parmesan, Swiss, Gruyere, Gouda)
dairy_and_alternatives.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A at normal serving - aging removes nearly all lactose
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Aging process removes lactose. Excellent calcium source for Crohn's patients. Important when on corticosteroids.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Brie, Camembert)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Soft but aged enough to be low lactose. Good choice.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Mozzarella)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Semi-soft but low lactose. Fresh mozzarella slightly higher in lactose than aged.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Feta)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Good flavor at small amounts.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Haloumi)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Good protein source.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Cottage)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Fresh cheese - higher lactose than aged. Small serving only.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Ricotta)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Fresh whey cheese - contains significant lactose. Lactose-free ricotta available.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cheese (Cream cheese)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Lactose-free cream cheese is preferred.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Butter
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Almost pure fat, virtually no lactose. Good calorie source.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Ghee / Clarified butter
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Zero lactose. Good for cooking at high heat.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Cream (heavy/whipping)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: High fat, some lactose. Small amounts in cooking OK.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Sour cream
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Small serving OK. Lactose-free versions preferred.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Ice cream (regular)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: High lactose and often contains HFCS. Lactose-free ice cream available.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Ice cream (lactose-free)
dairy_and_alternatives.high_fodmap_threshold: Check for chicory fiber/inulin in ingredients
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Watch for inulin/chicory root fiber which many brands add.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Kefir (regular)
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Fermentation reduces some lactose but not enough. Lactose-free kefir is available.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Whey protein isolate
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: ISOLATE only - whey protein CONCENTRATE is high FODMAP (contains lactose). Critical for Crohn's patients needing protein supplementation.

dairy_and_alternatives.name: Whey protein concentrate
dairy_and_alternatives.crohns_notes: Contains significant lactose. Choose isolate instead.

proteins.name: Beef (all cuts, plain)
proteins.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - no FODMAPs in plain meat
proteins.crohns_notes: Good iron and B12 source. Choose tender cuts. Ground beef is easiest to digest. Avoid if marinated with garlic/onion.

proteins.name: Chicken (all cuts, plain)
proteins.crohns_notes: Lean protein, easy to digest. Avoid if marinated/seasoned with garlic/onion.

proteins.name: Turkey (plain)
proteins.crohns_notes: Lean protein. Deli turkey - check for garlic/onion seasoning.

proteins.name: Pork (all cuts, plain)
proteins.crohns_notes: Good protein source. Avoid processed pork products with additives.

proteins.name: Lamb (all cuts, plain)
proteins.crohns_notes: Good iron source. May be higher in fat depending on cut.

proteins.name: Fish (salmon, tuna, cod, haddock, trout, halibut, etc.)
proteins.crohns_notes: Excellent omega-3 source (especially salmon, sardines, mackerel). Anti-inflammatory. Highly recommended for Crohn's patients.

proteins.name: Shellfish (shrimp, crab, lobster, mussels, oysters, scallops)
proteins.crohns_notes: Good zinc source. Canned/tinned varieties also safe.

proteins.name: Eggs
proteins.crohns_notes: Excellent protein source, easy to digest in most forms. Scrambled and poached are easiest on the gut.

proteins.name: Tofu (firm/extra-firm, drained)
proteins.crohns_notes: Draining and pressing removes water-soluble FODMAPs. SILKEN tofu is moderate-high FODMAP (more liquid, more GOS). Firm only.

proteins.name: Tofu (silken/soft)
proteins.crohns_notes: Higher in GOS than firm tofu because less pressing/draining.

proteins.name: Tempeh
proteins.crohns_notes: Fermentation reduces FODMAPs. Good plant protein source.

proteins.name: Deli meats / Cold cuts (plain, no garlic/onion)
proteins.crohns_notes: MUST check ingredients - many contain garlic powder, onion powder, or HFCS. Plain ham, turkey breast, prosciutto are usually safe.

proteins.name: Sausage / Chorizo
proteins.crohns_notes: Most commercial sausages contain garlic and/or onion. Look for specialty FODMAP-friendly brands or make your own.

proteins.name: Lentils (canned and drained)
proteins.crohns_notes: CANNED and DRAINED is critical - nearly 50% less FODMAPs than dried/cooked. FODMAPs leach into canning liquid. Rinse well.

proteins.name: Lentils (dried, cooked)
proteins.crohns_notes: Soak 12-24 hours and discard soaking water to reduce FODMAPs. Boil 30+ minutes. Red lentils are slightly better tolerated than green/brown.

proteins.name: Chickpeas (canned and drained)
proteins.crohns_notes: Small serving only. Canned and rinsed reduces GOS. Hummus from canned chickpeas: 2 tbsp is low FODMAP.

proteins.name: Chickpeas (dried, cooked)
proteins.crohns_notes: Very high GOS. Use canned/drained instead.

proteins.name: Black beans (canned and drained)
proteins.crohns_notes: Small canned/drained serving is OK. Rinse well.

proteins.name: Kidney beans / Butter beans / Lima beans
proteins.crohns_notes: Very high GOS. Even canned varieties remain high at normal servings.

proteins.name: Baked beans (canned)
proteins.crohns_notes: Sauce often contains onion, garlic, and HFCS in addition to high-GOS beans.

proteins.name: Edamame / Soybeans
proteins.crohns_notes: Whole soybeans are high FODMAP. Soy protein isolate products are OK.

proteins.name: Split peas
proteins.crohns_notes: High GOS. Pea soup is typically high FODMAP.

proteins.name: Quorn mince (mycoprotein)
proteins.crohns_notes: Check for onion/garlic in seasoned varieties. Plain mince is safe.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Almonds
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Must chew very well. Almond butter (1 tbsp) is easier to digest. Almond flour in large amounts (>1/4 cup) may be high FODMAP.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Almond butter
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Easier to digest than whole almonds. Good calorie source.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Brazil nuts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Excellent selenium source. Chew well.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Cashews
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Among the highest FODMAP nuts. Cashew milk and cashew cheese are also high FODMAP.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Chestnuts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Lower in fat than most nuts. Chestnut flour is high FODMAP in large amounts.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Hazelnuts / Filberts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Chew well. Hazelnut spread (Nutella) contains milk - check FODMAP.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Macadamia nuts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Among the safest nuts. High calorie/healthy fat. Good for underweight Crohn's patients.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Peanuts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Technically a legume but low FODMAP. Good protein source.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Peanut butter
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Check for added HFCS or honey. Plain/natural peanut butter is safest.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Pecans
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Good omega-3 source. Chew well.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Pine nuts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Good in pesto (garlic-free version).

nuts_and_seeds.name: Pistachios
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: High FODMAP like cashews. Avoid.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Walnuts
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Excellent omega-3 source. Anti-inflammatory. Good for Crohn's.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Chia seeds
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: High in soluble fiber (gel-forming). Can help with diarrhea. Omega-3 source. Soak before eating for best tolerance.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Flaxseed / Linseed
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Ground flaxseed is better absorbed. Good omega-3 source. Anti-inflammatory.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Hemp seeds
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Complete protein. Good omega-3/omega-6 ratio. Anti-inflammatory.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Poppy seeds
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Used in small amounts. Safe.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Pumpkin seeds / Pepitas
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Good zinc and magnesium source. Important minerals for Crohn's patients.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Sesame seeds
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Good calcium source. Tahini (sesame paste) is also low FODMAP at 2 tbsp.

nuts_and_seeds.name: Sunflower seeds
nuts_and_seeds.crohns_notes: Smaller safe serving than other seeds. Good vitamin E source.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Garlic-infused oil
condiments_and_sauces.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - fructans are water-soluble, NOT oil-soluble
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: ESSENTIAL for low FODMAP cooking. Provides garlic flavor without fructans. Must not contain garlic pieces - strain thoroughly. Commercial brands available.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Soy sauce / Tamari (gluten-free)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Safe flavor enhancer. GF tamari avoids wheat.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Fish sauce
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Good umami flavor source. Check for garlic in ingredients.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Oyster sauce
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Often contains wheat. Choose GF brand if needed.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Ketchup / Tomato sauce
condiments_and_sauces.high_fodmap_threshold: >2 tbsp (some brands contain HFCS or onion)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Check for HFCS, onion powder, garlic powder in ingredients.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Mustard (yellow/Dijon)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Safe condiment. Wholegrain mustard also OK.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Mayonnaise (no garlic/onion)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Check ingredients - many brands contain garlic. Homemade is safest.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Vinegar (all types: white, apple cider, balsamic, rice wine)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Apple cider vinegar may have probiotic benefits. Balsamic has more sugar - keep to 1-2 tbsp.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Maple syrup (pure)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Good honey substitute. Must be pure maple syrup, not maple-flavored (which may contain HFCS).

condiments_and_sauces.name: Honey
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: One of the highest fructose foods. Common in granola bars, cereals, dressings - check labels.

condiments_and_sauces.name: BBQ sauce (standard)
condiments_and_sauces.safe_serving: Not recommended unless certified low FODMAP brand
condiments_and_sauces.high_fodmap_threshold: Any serving (usually contains onion, garlic, honey/HFCS)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Almost all commercial BBQ sauces are high FODMAP. Specialty low-FODMAP brands exist.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Tomato paste / Puree
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Good base for sauces. Check for onion/garlic.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Miso paste
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Fermented soy product. Good umami flavor. May have probiotic benefits.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Pesto (standard with garlic)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Contains garlic and sometimes cashews. Make homemade with garlic-infused oil instead.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Hummus (standard)
condiments_and_sauces.safe_serving: 2 tbsp (50g) of canned-chickpea hummus may be low
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Often contains garlic. Small serving of homemade (garlic-free, canned chickpeas) may be OK.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Sriracha
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Contains garlic but in small amounts per tsp. Spicy foods may irritate Crohn's during flares.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Worcestershire sauce
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Contains traces of onion/garlic but very dilute at small serving.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Tahini (sesame paste)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Good calcium source. Useful in dressings and sauces.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Strawberry / Raspberry jam (no HFCS)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Must not contain HFCS, apple juice, or pear juice. Check ingredients.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Marmalade
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Citrus-based. Check for HFCS.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Stock cubes / Bouillon (commercial)
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Make homemade stock with green leek tops, chives, and other low-FODMAP aromatics instead.

condiments_and_sauces.name: Salad dressing (commercial)
condiments_and_sauces.high_fodmap_threshold: Most commercial dressings contain onion, garlic, honey, or HFCS
condiments_and_sauces.crohns_notes: Make your own with olive oil, vinegar/lemon, herbs, salt, pepper.

beverages.name: Water
beverages.crohns_notes: Essential. Crohn's patients are at higher risk of dehydration, especially with diarrhea. Aim for 8+ glasses daily.

beverages.name: Coffee (black, espresso)
beverages.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A for FODMAPs, but caffeine is a gut stimulant
beverages.crohns_notes: Coffee itself is low FODMAP but caffeine stimulates motility. May worsen diarrhea in Crohn's. Limit to 1-2 cups if symptomatic.

beverages.name: Tea (black, weak)
beverages.crohns_notes: Weak brew is key. Strong black tea becomes moderate FODMAP.

beverages.name: Tea (green)
beverages.crohns_notes: Anti-inflammatory polyphenols. Good choice for Crohn's.

beverages.name: Tea (peppermint)
beverages.crohns_notes: Peppermint has antispasmodic properties. Can help with cramping.

beverages.name: Tea (chamomile)
beverages.crohns_notes: Strong chamomile is high FODMAP. Weak brew may be tolerated.

beverages.name: Tea (chai, strong)
beverages.crohns_notes: Contains spices that may irritate. Weak brew tolerated by some.

beverages.name: Tea (fennel)
beverages.crohns_notes: Despite fennel bulb being OK, fennel tea concentrates fructans.

beverages.name: Tea (ginger, fresh)
beverages.crohns_notes: Excellent for nausea and inflammation. Highly recommended for Crohn's.

beverages.name: Orange juice
beverages.crohns_notes: Acidic - may irritate mouth ulcers. Small serving only.

beverages.name: Cranberry juice
beverages.crohns_notes: Check for added apple/pear juice concentrate which is high FODMAP.

beverages.name: Apple juice
beverages.crohns_notes: Very high fructose. Used as sweetener in many 'no added sugar' products - check labels.

beverages.name: Pear juice
beverages.crohns_notes: Like apple juice - very high FODMAP.

beverages.name: Mango juice
beverages.crohns_notes: Concentrated fructose.

beverages.name: Coconut water
beverages.crohns_notes: Good electrolyte source for rehydration but limited serving. Contains sorbitol.

beverages.name: Kombucha
beverages.crohns_notes: Despite probiotic benefits, high in FODMAPs from fermentation sugars.

beverages.name: Beer (standard)
beverages.crohns_notes: Brewing process breaks down fructans from wheat/barley. Carbonation may cause bloating. Alcohol is a gut irritant - use caution during flares.

beverages.name: Wine (red, white, sparkling)
beverages.crohns_notes: Dry wines are lower FODMAP than sweet. Sulfites may trigger symptoms in some. Alcohol suppresses immune function - consider with immunomodulators.

beverages.name: Wine (sweet/fortified/dessert: port, sherry, ice wine)
beverages.crohns_notes: Concentrated sugars. Avoid.

beverages.name: Gin
beverages.crohns_notes: Distillation removes FODMAPs. Mix with soda water and lime, not tonic (tonic may contain HFCS).

beverages.name: Vodka
beverages.crohns_notes: Safe spirit. Avoid mixers with HFCS or fruit juices.

beverages.name: Whiskey / Whisky
beverages.crohns_notes: Distillation removes FODMAPs from grain mash.

beverages.name: Rum
beverages.crohns_notes: Only spirit tested high FODMAP. High fructose load.

beverages.name: Soda / Soft drinks (with HFCS)
beverages.crohns_notes: HFCS is high FODMAP. Carbonation causes bloating.

beverages.name: Soda / Soft drinks (with sugar/sucrose, no HFCS)
beverages.crohns_notes: FODMAPs are fine but carbonation and sugar still problematic. Not recommended for gut health.

sweeteners.name: White sugar / Sucrose
sweeteners.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A at normal serving - sucrose is 50/50 glucose/fructose (balanced)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Low FODMAP because glucose and fructose are in equal ratio. Still limit for general health.

sweeteners.name: Brown sugar
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Same as white sugar with molasses added.

sweeteners.name: Maple syrup (pure)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Best honey alternative. Must be pure, not maple-flavored syrup.

sweeteners.name: Rice malt syrup
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Good low-FODMAP sweetener alternative. Contains glucose, no fructose.

sweeteners.name: Glucose / Dextrose
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Glucose is well-absorbed. Can actually help fructose absorption when present in equal or greater amounts.

sweeteners.name: Stevia
sweeteners.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - check for added polyols in blends
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Check blends - some contain erythritol or other bulking agents. Pure stevia is safe.

sweeteners.name: Aspartame
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Low FODMAP but controversial for gut health in general.

sweeteners.name: Sucralose (Splenda)
sweeteners.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A for FODMAPs - check for added maltodextrin
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Some research suggests sucralose may alter gut microbiome. Use cautiously with IBD.

sweeteners.name: Saccharin
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Low FODMAP.

sweeteners.name: Erythritol
sweeteners.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - better absorbed than other sugar alcohols
sweeteners.crohns_notes: The ONLY low-FODMAP sugar alcohol. Absorbed in small intestine (90%) so doesn't reach colon for fermentation.

sweeteners.name: Honey
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Very high excess fructose. One of the most common FODMAP triggers.

sweeteners.name: Agave nectar / Syrup
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Extremely high fructose despite being marketed as 'natural'. Worse than honey.

sweeteners.name: High fructose corn syrup (HFCS)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Found in many US processed foods. Check all labels. Major hidden FODMAP source.

sweeteners.name: Sorbitol (E420)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Found in sugar-free gum, mints, diabetic products. Strong osmotic laxative effect.

sweeteners.name: Mannitol (E421)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Found in sugar-free products. Osmotic laxative.

sweeteners.name: Xylitol (E967)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Common in sugar-free gum and toothpaste. Causes significant GI distress.

sweeteners.name: Maltitol (E965)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Common in sugar-free chocolate and candy. Known to cause severe diarrhea.

sweeteners.name: Isomalt (E953)
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Used in sugar-free hard candy. Contains both sorbitol and mannitol.

sweeteners.name: Inulin / FOS / Chicory root fiber
sweeteners.crohns_notes: CRITICAL: Added to many 'healthy' products as prebiotic fiber - protein bars, yogurts, ice cream, cereals. Check ALL processed food labels for inulin, chicory root fiber, chicory root extract, FOS, oligofructose.

sweeteners.name: Coconut sugar
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Small safe serving. Contains inulin at larger amounts.

sweeteners.name: Golden syrup
sweeteners.crohns_notes: Small amounts OK.

sweeteners.name: Molasses
sweeteners.crohns_notes: High fructose.

snack_foods.name: Plain potato chips / Crisps
snack_foods.high_fodmap_threshold: Check for onion/garlic powder in flavored varieties
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Plain salted only. Most flavored chips contain onion/garlic powder.

snack_foods.name: Corn chips / Tortilla chips (plain)
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Plain corn-based. Check for wheat in ingredients.

snack_foods.name: Rice crackers / Rice cakes
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Good safe snack base. Check flavored varieties for FODMAP ingredients.

snack_foods.name: Pretzels (wheat)
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Contains wheat but processing may reduce some fructans. Keep serving small.

snack_foods.name: Dark chocolate (70%+)
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Contains antioxidants. Caffeine content may stimulate bowel. Check for inulin in 'fiber-enriched' versions.

snack_foods.name: Milk chocolate
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Contains some lactose. Smaller safe serving than dark chocolate.

snack_foods.name: White chocolate
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Most lactose of the three types. Very small serving.

snack_foods.name: Popcorn (plain, air-popped)
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Hulls can irritate bowel. Avoid during flares. Avoid microwave popcorn with butter flavoring.

snack_foods.name: Granola bars / Cereal bars
snack_foods.safe_serving: Not recommended unless certified low FODMAP
snack_foods.high_fodmap_threshold: Most contain honey, HFCS, dried fruit, chicory fiber
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Almost all commercial bars are high FODMAP. Look for certified low-FODMAP bars.

snack_foods.name: Trail mix (standard)
snack_foods.high_fodmap_threshold: Usually contains cashews, pistachios, dried fruit
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Make your own with safe nuts (macadamia, peanuts, walnuts) and safe dried fruit (cranberries).

snack_foods.name: Sugar-free gum / mints
snack_foods.crohns_notes: Almost all contain sorbitol, xylitol, or mannitol. Common hidden FODMAP source.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Sourdough bread (spelt, long-fermented)
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Best bread option. Long fermentation (12-24 hours) breaks down fructans. MUST be genuinely slow-fermented - not commercial 'sourdough flavored'.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Sourdough bread (wheat, long-fermented)
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Better than regular wheat bread but not as low FODMAP as spelt sourdough.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: White bread (wheat, standard)
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Single slice may be tolerated. Normal 2-slice sandwich is high FODMAP.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Whole wheat / Wholemeal bread
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Higher in fructans AND insoluble fiber than white. Worse choice for Crohn's during flares.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Gluten-free bread
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Good option BUT check ingredients. Some GF breads add inulin/chicory root for fiber, making them high FODMAP despite being gluten-free.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Rye bread
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Very high fructans. Rye sourdough may be slightly better but still not recommended during elimination.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Corn bread
bread_and_baked_goods.high_fodmap_threshold: Depends on recipe - check for wheat flour, milk, honey
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Homemade with corn flour, safe milk, and safe sweetener is a good option.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Rice bread
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Good safe option. Check for additives.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Croissant
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Wheat flour and butter/milk. High fat may also trigger symptoms.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Tortilla (corn)
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Check for wheat flour addition. Pure corn tortillas are safe.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Tortilla (wheat/flour)
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Contains wheat. Use corn tortillas instead.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Pumpernickel bread
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Made from rye. Very high fructans.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Pancakes / Waffles (GF mix)
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Use GF flour, lactose-free milk, eggs. Top with maple syrup (not honey) and safe fruits.

bread_and_baked_goods.name: Rice paper wrappers
bread_and_baked_goods.crohns_notes: Good for spring rolls with low-FODMAP fillings.

oils_and_fats.name: Olive oil
oils_and_fats.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - no FODMAPs in pure oils
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: Anti-inflammatory oleic acid. Extra virgin has most polyphenols. Recommended for Crohn's.

oils_and_fats.name: Garlic-infused olive oil
oils_and_fats.high_fodmap_threshold: N/A - fructans are water-soluble, not oil-soluble
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: THE key cooking ingredient for low-FODMAP flavor. Ensure no garlic pieces remain in the oil.

oils_and_fats.name: Coconut oil
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: Contains medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) which are easily absorbed. Good for Crohn's patients with fat malabsorption.

oils_and_fats.name: Sunflower oil
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: High in omega-6; balance with omega-3 sources.

oils_and_fats.name: Butter
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: Almost pure fat. Safe. Good calorie source.

oils_and_fats.name: Ghee / Clarified butter
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: All milk solids removed. Zero lactose. Good for dairy-sensitive Crohn's patients.

oils_and_fats.name: Margarine
oils_and_fats.crohns_notes: Check for milk solids and whey in ingredients.

herbs_and_spices.name: Fresh herbs (basil, cilantro, dill, mint, oregano, parsley, rosemary, sage, thyme, tarragon, lemongrass)
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: All fresh herbs are low FODMAP and safe. Great for adding flavor without garlic/onion.

herbs_and_spices.name: Dried spices (black pepper, cinnamon, cumin, turmeric, paprika, ginger, cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, saffron, star anise, allspice, coriander seeds, fennel seeds, mustard seeds)
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: All safe. Turmeric and ginger have anti-inflammatory properties - excellent for Crohn's. Chili/cayenne may irritate during flares.

herbs_and_spices.name: Garlic powder / Garlic salt
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: Concentrated fructans. Hidden in many spice blends, seasoning mixes, and processed foods.

herbs_and_spices.name: Onion powder / Onion salt
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: Concentrated fructans. Check all spice blends and seasoning packets.

herbs_and_spices.name: Asafoetida (hing) powder
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: Provides onion/garlic-like flavor without FODMAPs. Key ingredient for Indian low-FODMAP cooking.

herbs_and_spices.name: Curry powder (check ingredients)
herbs_and_spices.safe_serving: Normal recipe amount if no onion/garlic
herbs_and_spices.high_fodmap_threshold: Check for onion/garlic powder in blend
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: Contains turmeric which is anti-inflammatory. Just verify no onion/garlic in the blend.

herbs_and_spices.name: Five spice powder
herbs_and_spices.crohns_notes: Traditional Chinese five spice is low FODMAP.

cooking_effects_on_fodmaps.description: How preparation and cooking methods change FODMAP content in foods

methods.effect: Reduces GOS and fructans by approximately 50%
methods.details: FODMAPs are water-soluble and leach into the canning liquid during storage. Draining and rinsing canned legumes removes the FODMAP-rich liquid.
examples: Canned lentils (drained): low FODMAP at 46g vs dried cooked lentils which are high FODMAP
Canned chickpeas (drained): low FODMAP at 42g (1/4 cup)
Canned black beans (drained): low FODMAP at 45g

methods.details: Soaking and discarding the soaking water removes some water-soluble FODMAPs. Less effective than canning but still beneficial. Always discard soaking water.
examples: Dried lentils soaked 12-24 hours then boiled: lower FODMAP than unsoaked
Dried chickpeas soaked overnight: reduced GOS

methods.details: Research shows boiling dried red lentils or kidney beans progressively lowers their FODMAP content every 5 minutes up to 30 minutes. Straining after cooking removes additional FODMAPs from the cooking liquid.
examples: Red lentils boiled 30+ minutes and drained: significantly lower FODMAPs
Kidney beans boiled and drained: reduced GOS

methods.details: Long, slow fermentation (12-24 hours) by sourdough cultures breaks down fructans in wheat and spelt flour. The lactic acid bacteria consume fructans as food. Mass-produced bread with 'sourdough flavoring' does NOT have reduced fructans.
examples: Spelt sourdough (long-ferment): low FODMAP at 2 slices
Wheat sourdough (long-ferment): lower FODMAP than regular wheat bread
Commercial quick-rise 'sourdough': NOT reduced - still high FODMAP

methods.effect: May reduce FODMAPs in some vegetables
methods.details: The pickling process can allow FODMAPs to leach into the brine. Pickled vegetables may have lower FODMAP content than fresh.
examples: Pickled beetroot: low FODMAP vs fresh beetroot which is high
Pickled gherkins: low FODMAP
Pickled onions (large, well-pickled): may be tolerated in small amounts

methods.details: Fructans are water-soluble but NOT oil-soluble. Heating garlic or onion in oil transfers flavor compounds to the oil without transferring fructans. The garlic/onion pieces must be completely removed.
examples: Garlic-infused olive oil: full garlic flavor, zero fructans
Onion-infused oil: onion flavor without FODMAPs

methods.details: As bananas ripen, resistant starch converts to fructans and free sugars. Green/firm bananas are low FODMAP; ripe (spotted) bananas are moderate to high FODMAP.
examples: Firm/slightly green banana: low FODMAP at 1 medium
Ripe/spotted banana: moderate FODMAP, reduce to 1/3 medium

methods.details: Similar to legumes, canned vegetables that sit in liquid will have some FODMAPs leach into the liquid. Draining reduces FODMAP content.
examples: Canned mushrooms (drained): lower mannitol than fresh mushrooms
Canned beetroot (drained): lower fructans than fresh

methods.effect: No significant change to FODMAP content
methods.details: Freezing does not significantly alter FODMAP levels in foods.
Removing water concentrates sugars including fructose and sorbitol per gram. Dried fruits are almost always higher FODMAP than fresh equivalents.
examples: Fresh pineapple (1 cup): low FODMAP. Dried pineapple: HIGH FODMAP
Fresh cranberries: low FODMAP. Dried cranberries: limit to 1 tbsp
Raisins, sultanas, prunes, dried apricots, dried mango: all HIGH FODMAP

fodmap_stacking_rules.description: How combining multiple FODMAP-containing foods in one meal affects total FODMAP load

key_principles.rule: Green (low) serves can be safely combined
key_principles.explanation: Monash's cut-off criteria were set conservatively. Multiple green-light serves of different foods can be combined in one meal without triggering symptoms for most people.

Combining two foods that are both moderate in the SAME FODMAP type (e.g., two fructose sources) is more likely to push you over your threshold than combining two different types (e.g., one fructose + one GOS source).

key_principles.rule: All FODMAP types DO stack together
key_principles.explanation: While same-type stacking is most risky, ALL FODMAP types can contribute to total fermentation load. Even different types (fructose + fructans + GOS) stack together at some level.

key_principles.rule: Limit moderate (amber) foods to one per meal
key_principles.explanation: As a practical guideline, include no more than one moderate-FODMAP food per meal. Spacing meals 2-3 hours apart allows the gut to process before the next FODMAP load.
Leave 2-3 hours between meals and snacks. This prevents FODMAPs from one meal combining with the next in the gut. FODMAPs from a meal typically reach the colon within 2-4 hours.

There are no universal stacking thresholds. Personal tolerance depends on gut bacteria composition, transit time, visceral sensitivity, and overall gut health. Crohn's patients typically have lower tolerance than IBS patients.

practical_examples.safe_combination: Sourdough bread (fructans: green) + cheddar cheese (lactose: green) + strawberries (fructose: green) + butter (no FODMAPs) = safe meal. All green serves from different FODMAP types.
practical_examples.risky_combination: Honeydew melon (fructose: green at 90g) + mango (fructose: green at 40g) + orange juice (fructose: green at 100ml) = potentially problematic. Three fructose sources stacking.
practical_examples.unsafe_combination: Avocado 1/4 (sorbitol: moderate) + sweet potato 100g (mannitol: moderate) + broccoli heads 100g (fructans: moderate) = likely high FODMAP meal. Three moderate serves in one sitting.

fodmap_stacking_rules.crohns_specific_note: Crohn's patients, especially those with active disease or post-resection, typically have LOWER FODMAP tolerance thresholds than IBS patients. Be more conservative with stacking during flares. Start with smaller portions and single-FODMAP-type meals during elimination phase.

phase_1_elimination.name: Elimination Phase
phase_1_elimination.description: Strictly reduce all high-FODMAP foods to determine if FODMAPs are causing symptoms. Replace high-FODMAP foods with low-FODMAP alternatives.
key_points: This is NOT a forever diet - it is a diagnostic tool
Work with a FODMAP-trained dietitian (essential for Crohn's patients who already risk malnutrition)
If symptoms improve significantly (typically 50-80% improvement), FODMAPs are likely a trigger
If no improvement after 6 weeks, FODMAPs are likely not the primary issue
Continue all IBD medications as prescribed - FODMAP diet does NOT replace medical treatment
phase_1_elimination.crohns_specific: Crohn's patients should only attempt elimination while in remission or near-remission. During active flares, focus on medical management first. The restrictive nature risks worsening malnutrition if not supervised.

phase_2_reintroduction.name: Reintroduction (Challenge) Phase
phase_2_reintroduction.description: Systematically test each FODMAP subgroup to identify which specific types trigger YOUR symptoms and at what dose.

protocol.instruction: Choose one FODMAP subgroup to test (e.g., fructose)
protocol.note: Keep background diet low FODMAP throughout

protocol.instruction: Day 1: small serve of test food (e.g., 1/2 tsp honey for fructose)
Day 2: medium serve of test food (e.g., 1 tsp honey)
Day 3: large/normal serve of test food (e.g., 1 tbsp honey)
Days 4-6: washout period - return to strict low FODMAP
protocol.note: Allow gut to reset before next challenge
Test all 6 subgroups: fructose, lactose, fructans, GOS, sorbitol, mannitol

challenge_foods_by_type.lactose: Regular milk (increasing from 1/4 cup to 1 cup)
challenge_foods_by_type.fructans_vegetables: Garlic (1/4 to 1 clove) or onion (increasing portions)

phase_2_reintroduction.crohns_specific: Crohn's patients may need slower reintroduction with smaller increments. Keep a detailed symptom diary. Distinguish between FODMAP reactions (gas, bloating, diarrhea within 2-6 hours) and Crohn's flare symptoms (bloody stool, fever, sustained pain).

phase_3_personalization.name: Personalization (Modified FODMAP) Phase
phase_3_personalization.description: Establish your individualized long-term diet based on reintroduction results. Only restrict the specific FODMAPs that triggered symptoms, at the doses that triggered them.
key_points: Liberalize diet as much as tolerated - more variety = better gut health
You may tolerate some high-FODMAP foods at certain portions
FODMAP tolerance can change over time - retest every 3-6 months
Stress, illness, menstruation, and sleep can temporarily lower tolerance
Aim for maximum dietary diversity to support microbiome health
The goal is the LEAST restrictive diet that controls symptoms
phase_3_personalization.crohns_specific: FODMAP tolerance may decrease during Crohn's flares and increase during remission. Re-evaluate triggers when disease state changes. Monitor nutritional status regularly - vitamin D, B12, iron, folate, calcium, and zinc are commonly deficient in Crohn's.

common_fodmap_mistakes.mistake: Treating low FODMAP as a permanent diet
common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: The elimination phase should last 2-6 weeks only. Long-term strict restriction reduces beneficial gut bacteria (especially bifidobacteria) and risks nutritional deficiencies.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Always progress to reintroduction and personalization phases. The goal is the LEAST restrictive diet.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Gluten-free products are not automatically low FODMAP. Many GF products contain inulin, chicory root fiber, honey, apple juice, or other high-FODMAP ingredients. Conversely, small amounts of wheat (1 slice bread) may be tolerated on low FODMAP.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Always check the FULL ingredient list, not just 'gluten-free' label.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Many foods are low FODMAP at one serving size but high at another. For example, sweet potato is low at 75g but high at 150g. Eating 'low FODMAP' foods in large portions defeats the purpose.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Weigh foods during elimination phase. Use a food scale. Follow Monash app serving sizes precisely.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Garlic powder, onion powder, honey, HFCS, inulin, and chicory root fiber hide in many processed foods: stock cubes, sauces, dressings, protein bars, cereals, flavored chips, marinades.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Read EVERY ingredient label during elimination. Cook from scratch when possible.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Eating multiple moderate-FODMAP foods in one meal, or multiple servings of low-FODMAP foods from the same FODMAP group, can push total intake above tolerance threshold.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Limit to one moderate-FODMAP food per meal. Space meals 2-3 hours apart. Vary FODMAP types across meals.

common_fodmap_mistakes.mistake: Avoiding ALL dairy instead of just high-lactose dairy
common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Hard/aged cheeses (cheddar, parmesan, Swiss) and butter are virtually lactose-free. Cutting all dairy eliminates key calcium sources unnecessarily.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Include aged cheeses and lactose-free dairy products. Only avoid high-lactose items (milk, yogurt, soft cheese, ice cream) unless using lactose-free versions.

common_fodmap_mistakes.mistake: Not distinguishing between onion/garlic bulb and infused oil
common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: People avoid all garlic/onion flavor when only the fructan-containing solid matters. Fructans are water-soluble but NOT oil-soluble, so garlic/onion-infused oils are safe.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Use garlic-infused oil and onion-infused oil freely. Also safe: green tops of spring onions/leeks, chives, asafoetida.

common_fodmap_mistakes.mistake: Eating canned legumes without draining and rinsing
common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: The canning liquid contains leached FODMAPs. Eating legumes with their liquid delivers a much higher FODMAP dose.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Always drain and rinse canned legumes thoroughly before use.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Honey is natural but very high FODMAP. Agave is organic but 90% fructose. Many 'health foods' (granola, kombucha, dried fruit, protein bars with chicory) are high FODMAP.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: FODMAP content has nothing to do with whether a food is natural, organic, or 'healthy'.

common_fodmap_mistakes.mistake: Following the diet without professional support
common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Self-directed FODMAP elimination risks over-restriction, nutritional deficiency, incorrect reintroduction, and psychological food anxiety. Especially dangerous for Crohn's patients who already risk malnutrition.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Work with a FODMAP-trained dietitian, especially if you have IBD. Many offer telehealth consultations.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: FODMAP tolerance changes over time based on stress, gut bacteria changes, disease activity, and other factors. What triggered symptoms 6 months ago may be tolerated now.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Re-challenge trigger foods every 3-6 months. Tolerance often improves once the gut has time to heal.

common_fodmap_mistakes.explanation: Monash University continuously tests and updates their database. Foods previously rated high may now be low at certain servings, and vice versa. For example, blueberry serving size was increased from 40g to 125g in recent updates.
common_fodmap_mistakes.correction: Use the Monash FODMAP app (regularly updated) rather than static printouts or old blog posts.

general_notes: The low-FODMAP diet was developed for IBS, not IBD. It manages SYMPTOMS (bloating, gas, diarrhea) but does NOT reduce inflammation.
50-70% of IBD patients have concurrent IBS-like symptoms that may respond to FODMAP reduction.
NEVER use FODMAP diet as a substitute for prescribed IBD medications (biologics, immunomodulators, etc.).
Crohn's patients are at higher risk of nutritional deficiencies - monitor B12, iron, folate, vitamin D, calcium, zinc, and magnesium.
The restrictive nature of FODMAP elimination can worsen already-existing malnutrition in Crohn's patients.
Work with BOTH a gastroenterologist AND a FODMAP-trained dietitian.
post_resection_considerations: After bowel resection, absorptive surface area is reduced. Prioritize nutrient-dense foods even within FODMAP constraints.
Bile acid malabsorption is common after ileal resection - may cause diarrhea independent of FODMAPs.
Short bowel syndrome risk: if significant bowel removed, dietary management is more complex than FODMAP alone.
Insoluble fiber tolerance is often reduced post-resection. Cook vegetables well, peel fruits, avoid raw salads initially.
Fat malabsorption may occur - MCT oil (coconut oil) is more easily absorbed than long-chain fats.
B12 absorption occurs in the terminal ileum - if resected, B12 injections may be needed regardless of diet.
Gradually increase fiber as healing progresses. Start with soluble fiber (oats, peeled cooked vegetables) before insoluble.

during_flare: Focus on medical management first, diet second
Low residue/low fiber foods: white rice, peeled potatoes, eggs, plain chicken, bananas, white bread (even if high FODMAP - caloric intake may take priority)
Avoid raw vegetables, seeds, nuts, popcorn, corn, dried fruit
Small, frequent meals rather than large meals
Stay hydrated - electrolyte drinks if diarrhea is severe
Consider liquid nutrition supplements if eating is difficult
during_remission: Introduce anti-inflammatory foods: omega-3 rich fish, turmeric, ginger, olive oil
Rebuild gut microbiome diversity through varied diet

foods_especially_beneficial_for_crohns.reason: Omega-3 fatty acids reduce inflammation. Anti-inflammatory effect well-documented in IBD research.
Easy to digest, nutrient-dense, may support gut lining repair. Use green leek tops and chives for flavor.
Anti-inflammatory and anti-nausea properties. Helps with medication side effects.
Curcumin has demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in IBD studies. Black pepper increases absorption 2000%.
Easy to digest, potassium-rich, binding effect for diarrhea, low FODMAP.
Safe, easy to digest, good calorie and nutrient density when peeled and well-cooked.
Soluble fiber soothes gut. Easy to digest. Good vehicle for adding calories (butter, maple syrup).
Probiotics support beneficial gut bacteria. Protein and calcium source.
Complete protein, easy to digest, versatile preparation methods.
Anti-inflammatory polyphenols. Calorie-dense for patients who need to gain weight.

medication_diet_interactions: Corticosteroids: Increase need for calcium and vitamin D. Prioritize hard cheese, lactose-free dairy, fortified plant milks.
Methotrexate: Increases folate need. Eat folate-rich foods: spinach (cooked), oranges, eggs.
Azathioprine/6-MP: Grapefruit may interact. Avoid or check with pharmacist.
Biologics (Humira, Remicade, etc.): No specific FODMAP interactions, but ensure adequate nutrition to support immune function.
Sulfasalazine: May reduce folate absorption. Supplement as directed.
Iron supplements: Take with vitamin C (orange juice at safe FODMAP serving) for better absorption. Avoid taking with calcium-rich foods.
